title: Clinical Decision-Making in Neurogenetics
description: A decision-making framework that follows the patient journey — choosing the first test, reading an ambiguous report, acting on a result, managing the diagnosis, and counseling the family — connecting genetic findings to real clinical care.
learningObjectives: Select panel vs. exome vs. genome (and trio vs. singleton) from phenotype, inheritance pattern, and turnaround needs
Counsel a family about a VUS — what it does and does not mean, and when re-contact is warranted
Recognize when a negative genetic result is not a true negative and choose the right next step
Distinguish symptomatic from disease-modifying treatment and locate guideline-based surveillance schedules
Map the reproductive decision points: prenatal diagnosis, PGT-M, cascade testing, and donor options
Communicate prognosis honestly under genotype–phenotype uncertainty and coordinate multidisciplinary care

sections.title: Choosing the First Test: Panel vs. Exome vs. Genome
sections.content:
The first test is a decision, not a default. Five branch points determine the right starting point. The [[diagnostic-yields|Diagnostic Yields]] module holds the full numbers; this section is the decision layer.

**1. How specific is the phenotype?** A tight, recognizable syndrome (e.g., classic Rett, tuberous sclerosis) points to **single-gene testing or a focused panel** — high pre-test probability. A broad or undifferentiated presentation (unexplained GDD/ID) points to **exome (or genome)**, which interrogates the whole coding space rather than betting on a short gene list.

**2. Are both parents available?** For severe, early-onset, de novo-enriched phenotypes (DEE, GDD with seizures, MCA), **trio** sequencing (proband + both parents) approximately doubles yield versus singleton — OR ~2.04 (Clark 2018) — and phases compound heterozygotes. When parents are available and the phenotype is severe and early-onset, default to trio.

**3. Does the picture suggest a repeat expansion?** Progressive ataxia, myotonic dystrophy, or a Huntington-like phenotype should trigger **dedicated repeat testing** (repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read). Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably detect trinucleotide/pentanucleotide expansions.

**4. MCA/dysmorphism or infantile spasms?** CMA retains first-tier value: ~15–25% in multiple congenital anomalies, and 14% in infantile epileptic spasms (IESS) (vs. WES 26%). See [[cnv-interpretation|CNV Interpretation]] for what CMA detects (CNVs, aneuploidy, UPD/AOH on SNP arrays) and misses (SNVs, balanced rearrangements, repeat expansions).

**5. How urgent is turnaround?** An acutely ill NICU neonate needs **rapid WGS/WES** (35–50% yield; Maron JAMA 2023) — speed is the point, because diagnosis changes management in 38–50% of cases.

| Clinical situation | First test | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Recognizable tight syndrome | Single-gene / focused panel | High pre-test probability; fast, cheap |
| Undifferentiated GDD/ID, parents available | Trio exome (± concurrent CNV-seq) | ~2× yield (OR ~2.04, Clark 2018); de novo detection |
| Progressive ataxia / DM / HD-like | Dedicated repeat testing | Short-read WES/WGS misses expansions |
| MCA / dysmorphism | CMA first-tier | ~15–25% yield; detects CNVs/aneuploidy/UPD |
| Infantile epileptic spasms (IESS) | CMA + WES | CMA 14%, WES 26% (diagnostic-yields) |
| Acutely ill NICU neonate | Rapid WGS/WES | 35–50%; management changes 38–50% (Maron 2023) |

**Bottom line:** for most undifferentiated NDD/epilepsy with parents available, modern first-tier is **trio exome (± concurrent CNV-seq)**; CMA stays first-tier for MCA/dysmorphism; targeted panels fit phenotypically tight presentations; repeat disorders and NICU urgency each demand their own pathway.
keyPoints: Branch on phenotype specificity: tight recognizable syndrome -> single-gene/focused panel; broad/undifferentiated NDD -> exome (or genome)
For severe early-onset de novo-enriched phenotypes (DEE/GDD/MCA) with parents available, default to trio — ~doubles yield, OR ~2.04 (Clark 2018)
Repeat-expansion suspicion (progressive ataxia, DM1, Huntington) needs dedicated repeat testing; short-read WES/WGS does not reliably detect expansions
CMA stays first-tier for MCA/dysmorphism (~15–25%) and IESS (CMA 14% vs. WES 26%, diagnostic-yields)
Acutely ill NICU neonate -> rapid WGS/WES (35–50%; management changes in 38–50%, Maron JAMA 2023)

sections.title: Reading the Report: Living with a VUS
sections.content:
A **Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS)** is exactly that: a variant for which the available evidence is insufficient to call it pathogenic or benign. It is NOT a partial diagnosis, a 'weak positive,' or a hedge — it is the honest statement that we do not yet know. How the lab arrives at this tier (the ACMG/AMP evidence codes) is covered in [[variant-interpretation|Variant Interpretation]]; this section is about what you do with one in the room.

**The cardinal rule: clinical decisions are not made on a VUS.** Under the ACMG/AMP 2015 standards (Richards et al. 2015), a VUS must not be used to confirm or exclude a diagnosis. Do not change management, initiate surveillance, alter treatment, or drive reproductive decisions on an unresolved VUS. Manage the patient on their clinical findings — as if the VUS had not been reported.

**Reclassification skews benign.** When VUS are later reclassified, the majority move toward benign rather than pathogenic. A VUS is therefore not 'probably the answer,' and presenting it as the likely cause manufactures false certainty that can harm the family.

**What to say vs. what not to say:**

| Say this | Not this |
|---|---|
| "We found a genetic spelling variation we can't yet interpret." | "We found a mutation." |
| "It does not confirm a diagnosis, and it does not rule one out." | "We found the cause." |
| "We'll manage your child on their symptoms, not on this result." | "We should start treatment for this." |
| "Our understanding may change as evidence grows." | "It's nothing / it's definitely the problem." |

**What can move a VUS over time:** periodic lab reclassification as databases grow; segregation and parental (trio) testing — confirming de novo status is often the single highest-yield step; deeper phenotyping; and functional or RNA studies. Set honest expectations about re-contact: responsibility for notifying you of a reclassification — lab versus ordering clinician — is **not standardized**. Do not promise the family an automatic system will reach them. Document the VUS with explicit uncertainty language and own the plan to revisit it (commonly reanalysis in 1–2 years).
keyPoints: A VUS means the evidence is insufficient to call pathogenic or benign — it is genuinely uncertain, not a partial or 'weak' diagnosis
Cardinal rule (ACMG/AMP 2015, Richards et al.): never base management, surveillance, treatment, or reproductive decisions on an unresolved VUS — manage on clinical findings
When VUS are reclassified, most move toward benign, not pathogenic — so a VUS should not be treated as 'probably the answer'
Framing matters: say 'a genetic spelling variation we can't yet interpret; it doesn't confirm a diagnosis' — never 'we found a mutation / we found the cause'

Parental/segregation testing, deeper phenotyping, functional/RNA studies, and periodic lab reclassification can move a VUS — but re-contact responsibility (lab vs. clinician) is not standardized, so document the VUS and own the plan to reanalyze

sections.title: When "Negative" Isn't Negative
sections.content:
A negative report is **time-stamped, not permanent**. It means no diagnostic variant was found *with today's knowledge, on this platform, in this tissue* — not that a genetic cause is excluded. Before declaring the workup done, run the phenotype past four under-the-radar blind spots, each with its own fix — see [[diagnostic-yields|Diagnostic Yields]] for the reanalysis and platform-yield numbers.

| What was missed | Why standard testing missed it | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| Real diagnosis, immature database | Gene-disease knowledge at the time of the original report didn't yet explain the variant | **Reanalysis** of existing exome data at 12–24 months — new diagnoses in ~10–25% of previously unsolved cases. The raw data didn't change; the interpretation framework did |
| Repeat expansion | Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably size trinucleotide/pentanucleotide expansions | **Dedicated repeat testing** — repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read sequencing |
| Methylation / imprinting disorder | Not visible in sequence data alone — the defect is parent-of-origin methylation or UPD, not a coding variant | **Methylation-specific testing** (e.g., MS-MLPA at SNRPN) + **SNP-array CMA** for UPD |
| Mosaicism / wrong tissue | Somatic variant absent or very low-level in blood | **Deep-coverage sequencing** and/or sequencing of **affected tissue** (skin/biopsy) |

**The repeat-expansion blind spot — know the list.** Standard short-read sequencing misses: Friedreich ataxia (FXN GAA), spinocerebellar ataxias (CAG), CANVAS (RFC1 AAGGG), FXTAS (FMR1 CGG premutation), myotonic dystrophy DM1/DM2, Huntington disease (HTT CAG), and C9orf72 (ALS/FTD). A progressive ataxia, a myotonic or Huntington-like picture, or unexplained adult-onset tremor/ataxia should send you to dedicated repeat testing regardless of a 'negative' exome.

**Methylation and imprinting.** Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes — and other imprinting disorders — are driven by methylation defects or UPD that sequence reads alone cannot see. The SNRPN methylation test detects ~99% of PWS and ~80% of AS; a normal result in a classic Angelman picture still prompts UBE3A sequencing — the [[epigenetics|Methylation & Imprinting]] module covers the parent-of-origin mechanics in detail.

**Mosaicism and tissue choice.** Somatic mosaic overgrowth (e.g., PIK3CA, AKT3) and brain-restricted variants causing focal cortical dysplasia or hemimegalencephaly may be absent from blood entirely. The route is deep-coverage sequencing of the affected tissue — skin, biopsy, or resected cortex — not a repeat of the blood test, as the [[mosaicism|Somatic Mosaicism]] module details.

**Below the detection floor.** Deep-intronic, regulatory, and structural variants below standard WES detection are next-step territory for genome sequencing or RNA-seq.

**The clinical reflex:** after every negative result, ask *which of these blind spots fits this phenotype?* before calling the workup complete.
keyPoints: A negative report is time-stamped, not permanent: it reflects today's knowledge, this platform, and this tissue — not exclusion of a genetic cause
Database immaturity: reanalysis of existing exome data at 12–24 mo yields new diagnoses in ~10–25% of previously unsolved cases (diagnostic-yields) — same raw data, updated interpretation

Repeat-expansion blind spot: short-read WES/WGS misses Friedreich (FXN GAA), SCA (CAG), CANVAS (RFC1 AAGGG), FXTAS (FMR1 CGG premutation), DM1/DM2, Huntington (HTT CAG), C9orf72 — fix with repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read

Imprinting disorders (Angelman, Prader-Willi) need methylation-specific testing (MS-MLPA) + SNP-array CMA for UPD — invisible to sequence alone; somatic overgrowth (PIK3CA, AKT3) needs deep-coverage or affected-tissue sequencing (blood may miss it)

Clinical reflex: after a negative result, ask 'which blind spot fits this phenotype?' — and consider genome sequencing or RNA-seq for deep-intronic/regulatory/structural variants below standard WES detection

sections.title: After the Diagnosis: Treatment & Surveillance
sections.content:
A molecular diagnosis is not the end of the workup — it reframes management.

**Disease-modifying vs. symptomatic.** A **disease-modifying** therapy alters the underlying biology or natural history; **symptomatic/supportive** care treats the manifestations without changing the course. For a growing list of monogenic conditions, a precise molecular diagnosis is the gateway to disease-modifying treatment — see [[therapies|Therapies]] and [[neuromuscular|Neuromuscular Disease]]. In SMA, SMN-restoring therapy (nusinersen, an intrathecal ASO; risdiplam, an oral SMN2 splicing modifier; onasemnogene abeparvovec, AAV9-SMN1 gene replacement) transforms the natural history and is most effective given presymptomatically. In DMD, exon-skipping ASOs (e.g., eteplirsen for exon-51-amenable deletions) restore the reading frame in eligible genotypes. None of these can be offered without the exact molecular result.

**Precision symptomatic / metabolic treatment.** Even when no disease-modifying drug exists, the genotype often dictates the right symptomatic choice — and the wrong one to avoid (see [[epilepsy|Epilepsy]] and [[iem|Inborn Errors of Metabolism]]). GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1) responds to the **ketogenic diet**; pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) responds to **pyridoxine (B6)**. The genotype also flags drugs to *avoid*: in SCN1A/Dravet, **avoid sodium-channel blockers** (oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine), which worsen seizures; in SLC6A1, **valproate is first-line** (do not confuse with SCN1A); in ALDH5A1/SSADH, **avoid vigabatrin** (paradoxical GABA elevation). The molecular diagnosis thus unlocks targeted therapy, flags contraindicated drugs, and ends the diagnostic odyssey.

**Surveillance: the diagnosis triggers a program.** A confirmed genetic diagnosis activates a defined surveillance schedule for known complications — a core reason genetic diagnosis changes management. Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is the model, with clear international consensus (the 2021 International TSC Surveillance and Management recommendations, Northrup et al. 2021); see [[neurodevelopmental-disorders|Neurodevelopmental Disorders]] for TSC clinical detail.

| Organ system | What to monitor | Interval (Northrup 2021) |
|---|---|---|
| Brain | SEGA (subependymal giant cell astrocytoma) | MRI every 1–3 yr if asymptomatic and < 25 yr |
| Kidney | Angiomyolipoma, renal cysts | MRI every 1–3 yr, lifelong |
| Neurodevelopment | TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders) | Annual screen; full evaluation at key developmental ages |
| Heart | Cardiac rhabdomyoma | Echocardiogram every 1–3 yr in asymptomatic children until regression; ECG every 3–5 yr, all ages |
| Eyes | Retinal lesions; vigabatrin visual-field toxicity | Annual ophthalmologic exam |
| Skin / teeth | Skin lesions; dental review | Annual skin exam; dental review at least every 6 months |

**Bottom line:** after a diagnosis, ask three questions — is there a disease-modifying therapy, does the genotype change symptomatic drug choices (including drugs to avoid), and what surveillance does this diagnosis now mandate?
keyPoints: Disease-modifying therapy alters the disease course; symptomatic care treats manifestations — and a precise molecular diagnosis is the gateway to disease-modifying options (matches therapies module)

SMA is disease-modifiable by SMN restoration — nusinersen (intrathecal ASO), risdiplam (oral SMN2 splicing modifier), onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9-SMN1); DMD by exon-skipping ASOs such as eteplirsen for exon-51-amenable deletions (matches therapies + neuromuscular modules)
Genotype-directed symptomatic treatment: ketogenic diet for GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1); pyridoxine (B6) for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) (matches epilepsy + iem modules)

Genotype flags drugs to avoid: avoid sodium-channel blockers (oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine) in SCN1A/Dravet; valproate is first-line in SLC6A1 (not to be confused with SCN1A); avoid vigabatrin in ALDH5A1/SSADH (matches epilepsy module exactly)

A confirmed genetic diagnosis triggers a defined surveillance program for known complications — e.g., TSC has international consensus (Northrup et al. 2021): brain MRI every 1–3 yr if asymptomatic and < 25 yr, renal MRI every 1–3 yr lifelong, annual TAND screening, echocardiogram every 1–3 yr in asymptomatic children until rhabdomyoma regression, ECG every 3–5 yr

After a diagnosis, ask three questions: is there a disease-modifying therapy, does the genotype change symptomatic drug choices (including drugs to avoid), and what surveillance does this diagnosis now mandate?

sections.title: The Family: Reproductive & Cascade Decisions
sections.content:
A molecular diagnosis is rarely about one patient — it reshapes risk for the whole family. The full mechanics of these options live in [[genetic-counseling|Genetic Counseling]]; this section is the decision layer.

**Start by naming the recurrence-risk scenario.** The same diagnosis carries very different reproductive risk depending on how the variant arose:

- **Inherited** (one or both parents carry it): risk follows the inheritance pattern — 50% for autosomal dominant, 25% for autosomal recessive, and modified by penetrance and expressivity.
- **Apparently de novo** (absent in both parents' blood): empiric recurrence risk to a future pregnancy is **low but NOT zero**, because of possible parental **germline (gonadal) mosaicism** — commonly cited around ~1% for many neurodevelopmental conditions, though it varies by disorder (e.g., ~0.5–1% for MECP2/Rett, but ~7–14% for DMD). The mechanism — a variant enriched in a clinically normal parent's germ cells but absent from blood — is detailed in [[mosaicism|Somatic Mosaicism]]. Never counsel 'zero risk' from negative parental blood testing alone.

**Cascade testing.** Once a familial pathogenic variant is identified, offer targeted single-site testing to at-risk relatives. Counseling nuances: testing minors for adult-onset conditions without childhood actionability is generally deferred until autonomous consent; respect the right not to know; and obtain consent rather than assuming relatives want the result.

**Reproductive options when the family variant is known:**

| Family situation | Option | Key consideration |
|---|---|---|
| Wants definitive fetal diagnosis in an established pregnancy | CVS (10–13 wk) or amniocentesis (15–20 wk) | Diagnostic, not screening; ~0.1–0.3% miscarriage risk |
| Wants to avoid decisions about an established pregnancy | PGT-M with IVF | Tests embryos pre-transfer; needs known variant + custom probe (~4–6 wk); cost and IVF burden |
| Priority is avoiding transmission entirely | Donor gametes, embryo donation, or adoption | Removes the genetic risk from the affected parent's line |

**Tie the option to the biology.** Inheritance pattern and penetrance frame how a relative weighs these paths — a near-fully-penetrant dominant condition reads very differently from a low-penetrance or recessive one. The counselor's role is non-directive: present balanced options, not a steer.
keyPoints: Name the recurrence scenario first: inherited risk follows the inheritance pattern (AD 50%, AR 25%, modified by penetrance/expressivity), whereas apparently de novo is a different conversation

After an apparently de novo variant (absent in both parents' blood), recurrence risk is low but NOT zero due to possible parental germline (gonadal) mosaicism — commonly ~1% for many neurodevelopmental conditions, varying by disorder (~0.5–1% MECP2/Rett, ~7–14% DMD per mosaicism module); never counsel 'zero risk' from negative parental blood alone

Cascade testing offers targeted single-site testing to at-risk relatives — but defer testing minors for adult-onset conditions without childhood actionability, respect the right not to know, and obtain informed consent (matches genetic-counseling module)

Prenatal diagnosis with a known variant: CVS (10–13 wk) or amniocentesis (15–20 wk), diagnostic with ~0.1–0.3% procedure-related miscarriage risk; PGT-M with IVF tests embryos before transfer (needs known variant + custom probe ~4–6 wk) and avoids decisions about an established pregnancy

Donor gametes, embryo donation, or adoption are the options when avoiding transmission is the overriding priority; option choice is framed by inheritance pattern and penetrance, and counseling is non-directive

sections.title: Communicating Uncertainty & Coordinating Care
sections.content:
A gene name is rarely a precise prognosis. The same molecular diagnosis can produce dramatically different trajectories, and four forces drive that uncertainty: **variable expressivity** (the same variant is mild in one person and severe in another), **incomplete penetrance** (some carriers stay unaffected), **small-n genotypes** (only a handful of cases ever reported), and **ascertainment bias** — the earliest published cohorts skew toward the most severely affected, so the literature can read worse than reality once milder cases surface. Naming these forces is itself honest counseling — the principles of disclosure and non-directiveness live in [[genetic-counseling|Genetic Counseling]] and are applied to real families in [[virtual-cases|Virtual Cases]].

**Heuristics for the prognosis conversation.** Anchor explicitly on what is known versus unknown. Avoid false precision: give developmental ranges and the next milestones to watch rather than hard ceilings. Revisit the prognosis as the phenotype evolves — early prognosis is provisional. For an ultra-rare genotype, the honest answer is often 'we will learn together,' which builds more trust than a confident guess.

**How to phrase it:**

| Better | Worse |
|---|---|
| Children with this change vary widely; we'll track development and update you. | Your child will never walk or talk. |
| We don't set a limit on what your child can achieve. | This gene means severe disability. |
| Early reports show the most severe cases; milder ones may be under-reported. | The textbook says the outcome is poor. |
| Let's focus on the next milestone and reassess. | Here is the fixed ceiling for this diagnosis. |

**The diagnosis starts a coordinated program.** A genetic result is the beginning of a multidisciplinary plan, not the end of one. A typical team pairs clinical genetics and counseling with neurology, the therapies (PT, OT, speech-language pathology), and the organ specialists the syndrome demands — cardiology, nephrology, ophthalmology — plus developmental-behavioral support, palliative care where appropriate, and the family as a core partner. One clinician should serve as quarterback in a medical-home model: owning the problem list, synchronizing the specialists, and preventing care from fragmenting. Plan early for the pediatric-to-adult transition, a known point of dropout. The goal is a single coordinated plan, not a stack of disconnected referrals.
keyPoints: A gene name is rarely a precise prognosis: variable expressivity, incomplete penetrance, small-n genotypes, and ascertainment bias (early cohorts skew severe) all mean the same diagnosis yields a wide range of outcomes
Counsel honestly by anchoring on known vs. unknown, giving developmental ranges and next milestones instead of hard ceilings, and revisiting prognosis as the phenotype evolves

Avoid false precision and never-statements: prefer 'children with this change vary widely; we'll track and update' over 'your child will never walk/talk'; for ultra-rare genotypes, 'we will learn together' is the honest answer

The molecular diagnosis launches a coordinated multidisciplinary program — clinical genetics/counseling, neurology, therapies (PT/OT/SLP), syndrome-specific organ specialists, developmental-behavioral and palliative support, with the family as a core partner
One clinician should quarterback a medical-home model to keep care from fragmenting, and the pediatric-to-adult transition must be planned early as a known point of dropout

inlineQuiz.question: A 2-year-old presents with severe, undifferentiated global developmental delay and seizures and no recognizable syndrome. Both biological parents are available for testing. Which first test is best supported by the evidence?
options: Singleton whole exome sequencing (proband only), adding parents later only if a candidate variant is found
Chromosomal microarray alone, since it is the established first-tier test for neurodevelopmental disorders
Trio exome sequencing (proband + both parents), with concurrent CNV-seq
Stepwise single-gene testing for the most common epilepsy genes before any broad sequencing
inlineQuiz.explanation: A broad, undifferentiated NDD phenotype with seizures and both parents available is the textbook case for trio exome (± concurrent CNV-seq): the presentation is de novo-enriched and severe, and trio analysis approximately doubles yield versus singleton (OR ~2.04, Clark 2018) while phasing compound heterozygotes. Singleton WES is roughly half as effective for de novo-enriched phenotypes and forces costly follow-up parental testing. CMA alone (~10% pooled NDD yield) would miss the majority of diagnoses here — it stays first-tier for MCA/dysmorphism, not undifferentiated GDD. Stepwise single-gene testing fits a tight, recognizable syndrome with high pre-test probability, not a broad presentation, and only delays diagnosis.

inlineQuiz.question: A child with epilepsy has a multigene panel return a Variant of Uncertain Significance in a gene relevant to the phenotype. The family asks what this means for treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start disease-specific treatment for the condition linked to that gene, since a variant was identified
Tell the family the genetic cause has been found and begin condition-specific surveillance
Make no management change based on the VUS; explain the uncertainty and document a plan to reanalyze
Treat the VUS as likely pathogenic, because most VUS are eventually reclassified as disease-causing
inlineQuiz.explanation: Under the ACMG/AMP 2015 standards (Richards et al.), a VUS must not be used to confirm or exclude a diagnosis: do not change management, start treatment, or initiate surveillance on an unresolved VUS — manage the patient on their clinical findings as if it had not been reported. Telling the family the cause is found manufactures false certainty; when VUS are later reclassified, the majority move toward benign, not pathogenic, so treating it as 'probably the answer' is backwards. The honest framing is that this is a genetic variation we cannot yet interpret — it neither confirms nor rules out a diagnosis. Document the VUS with explicit uncertainty language and own a plan to revisit it (commonly reanalysis in 1–2 years), since re-contact responsibility is not standardized.

inlineQuiz.question: A 16-year-old with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and sensory neuropathy has trio whole exome sequencing return negative. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Accept the negative WES as having excluded a genetic cause of the ataxia
Order dedicated repeat-expansion testing (e.g., RFC1/CANVAS, FXN)
Repeat the same WES at a different laboratory, since platform differences likely explain the negative
Proceed directly to an unrelated muscle biopsy before any further genetic testing
inlineQuiz.explanation: Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably size trinucleotide/pentanucleotide repeat expansions, and the most common hereditary ataxias are repeat disorders — Friedreich ataxia (FXN GAA) and CANVAS (RFC1 biallelic AAGGG) in particular, the latter classically causing ataxia plus sensory neuropathy exactly as here. A negative exome in ataxia is time-stamped, not exclusionary, so accepting it as final misses a treatable diagnostic category. Repeating the same short-read WES elsewhere reproduces the same blind spot — the issue is platform scope, not lab quality. The right move is dedicated repeat testing (repeat-primed PCR, Southern blot, or long-read), not jumping to an unrelated test before the obvious blind spot is addressed.

inlineQuiz.question: A toddler receives a new molecular diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and is currently asymptomatic. Per the 2021 International TSC surveillance recommendations (Northrup et al.), which surveillance is now indicated?
options: Brain CT every 5 years to screen for SEGA, with renal ultrasound only if symptoms develop
Baseline and serial brain MRI every 1–3 years for SEGA, plus renal MRI every 1–3 years
Brain MRI only once at diagnosis, with no further imaging unless seizures worsen
Annual abdominal CT for angiomyolipoma, with no brain imaging until adulthood
inlineQuiz.explanation: A confirmed TSC diagnosis activates a defined surveillance program (Northrup et al. 2021): brain MRI every 1–3 years for subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) while asymptomatic and under 25 years, and renal MRI every 1–3 years, lifelong, for angiomyolipoma. MRI — not CT — is the recommended modality, avoiding cumulative ionizing radiation, so the CT-based options are wrong on modality and interval. Imaging only once at diagnosis abandons the serial monitoring that is the entire point of a surveillance schedule. The schedule also adds annual TAND screening, echocardiography every 1–3 years in asymptomatic children until rhabdomyoma regression, and annual ophthalmologic exam — the diagnosis triggers a coordinated program, not a single scan.

inlineQuiz.question: A couple has a known familial pathogenic variant and is planning a future pregnancy. They want to reduce recurrence risk but specifically wish to avoid facing decisions about an already-established pregnancy. Which option best fits their stated goal?
options: Amniocentesis at 15–20 weeks in a spontaneous pregnancy
Chorionic villus sampling at 10–13 weeks in a spontaneous pregnancy
Preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disease (PGT-M) with IVF
No effective options exist once a familial pathogenic variant is known
inlineQuiz.explanation: PGT-M with IVF tests embryos before transfer, so unaffected embryos are selected pre-pregnancy — directly meeting the couple's goal of avoiding decisions about an established pregnancy (it requires the known variant plus a custom probe, ~4–6 weeks to design, and carries IVF burden and cost). Both CVS (10–13 wk) and amniocentesis (15–20 wk) are diagnostic prenatal tests performed in an already-established pregnancy, which is precisely what this couple wants to avoid. 'No options available' is simply false: once the familial variant is known, prenatal diagnosis, PGT-M, and donor/adoption pathways are all on the table. The counselor's role is to present these non-directively, matched to the inheritance pattern and penetrance.

inlineQuiz.question: Parents of a child with an ultra-rare genotype reported in only a handful of cases ask, 'Will my child walk?' Which communication approach is most appropriate?
options: Quote the most severely affected published case as the expected outcome to prepare the family
Reassure them that development will be normal so they do not lose hope
Decline to discuss prognosis until many more cases of the genotype are published
Give honest developmental ranges, identify the next milestones to track, and plan to revisit as the phenotype evolves
inlineQuiz.explanation: For a small-n genotype, the honest approach is to anchor on what is known versus unknown, give developmental ranges and the next milestones to watch rather than hard ceilings, and revisit prognosis as the phenotype evolves. Quoting the worst published case imports ascertainment bias — the earliest cohorts skew toward the most severely affected, so the literature reads worse than reality once milder cases surface. Promising normal development is equally false precision and erodes trust when contradicted. Refusing to discuss abandons the family at the moment they need guidance; 'we will learn together' builds more trust than either a confident guess or silence, given variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.

quiz.question: A 3-week-old in the NICU has rapidly worsening encephalopathy, intractable seizures, and lactic acidosis of unclear cause; the neonatologist needs a result fast enough to guide acute management. Both parents are at the bedside. Which first-line genetic test best fits this situation?
options: A send-out chromosomal microarray, accepting a multi-week turnaround as the standard first-tier test
Rapid trio whole genome or exome sequencing, prioritizing speed because a diagnosis can change acute management
Stepwise single-gene testing of mitochondrial genes one at a time until a result returns
Dedicated repeat-expansion testing, since lactic acidosis points to a trinucleotide repeat disorder
quiz.explanation: An acutely ill neonate whose management hinges on a fast answer is the textbook indication for rapid trio WGS/WES, which yields a diagnosis in 35–50% of NICU cases (Maron JAMA 2023) and changes acute management in 38–50% of those diagnosed — the highest clinical utility in pediatric genetics. Speed is the point: results in days let the team start targeted therapy, avoid harmful drugs, or redirect care during the critical window. A send-out CMA is too slow and detects only CNVs/aneuploidy/UPD, missing the SNVs that drive most of these metabolic encephalopathies. Sequential single-gene testing wastes the very time that makes testing useful here. Lactic acidosis suggests a mitochondrial or metabolic disorder, not a repeat expansion — repeat testing is for progressive ataxia, myotonic, or Huntington-like pictures, not this presentation.

quiz.question: A healthy couple's first child carries a VUS in a neurodevelopmental gene. Now expecting a second child, they ask the obstetrician to perform prenatal testing for that VUS so they can 'know whether this baby is affected too.' How should the team respond?
options: Offer prenatal testing for the VUS and counsel that a positive fetal result would confirm the disorder
Explain that clinical and reproductive decisions are not made on a VUS, so prenatal testing for it is not indicated; pursue reclassification efforts instead
Reassure them the VUS is almost certainly pathogenic and recommend they consider pregnancy termination if the fetus carries it
Begin presymptomatic surveillance imaging in the affected child to clarify the VUS before the pregnancy is tested
quiz.explanation: Under the ACMG/AMP 2015 standards (Richards et al.), a VUS must not be used to confirm or exclude a diagnosis or to drive reproductive decisions — it is genuinely uncertain, not a 'weak positive.' Prenatal testing for an unresolved VUS cannot yield an interpretable answer: a fetus carrying it would still have a variant of unknown meaning, manufacturing false certainty and potentially harmful decisions. When VUS are later reclassified, the majority move toward benign, so treating it as 'almost certainly pathogenic' is backwards, and recommending termination on that basis is indefensible. The constructive path is reclassification work — parental/segregation testing (confirming de novo status is often the single highest-yield step), deeper phenotyping, and periodic lab reanalysis — not acting clinically on the VUS. Starting surveillance imaging in the child would also be acting on a VUS and is equally inappropriate.

quiz.question: A 45-year-old man develops progressive distal weakness, grip myotonia, early cataracts, and cardiac conduction disease; his father had similar adult-onset symptoms. A broad neuromuscular exome panel returns no diagnostic variant. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Conclude that the exome has excluded a hereditary cause and stop genetic testing
Order dedicated testing for the DMPK CTG repeat expansion (myotonic dystrophy type 1)
Repeat the same short-read exome at a second laboratory to confirm the negative
Send methylation-specific testing, since the multisystem picture suggests an imprinting disorder
quiz.explanation: Grip myotonia, distal weakness, early cataracts, cardiac conduction disease, and autosomal dominant adult onset are classic for myotonic dystrophy type 1, caused by a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK. Short-read WES/WGS does NOT reliably size trinucleotide/pentanucleotide expansions, so a 'negative' exome here is a known blind spot, not exclusion — the fix is dedicated repeat testing (repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot for the DMPK CTG repeat). Accepting the negative as final misses a diagnosis with direct implications for cardiac surveillance and family counseling. Repeating the same short-read platform elsewhere reproduces the identical blind spot — the limitation is platform scope, not lab quality. Methylation testing targets imprinting disorders such as Angelman/Prader-Willi, which this phenotype does not suggest.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old has severe intellectual disability, near-absent speech, a happy affect with frequent unprovoked laughter, ataxic gait, and epilepsy. Trio exome sequencing, which included UBE3A, returns negative. Which next test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
options: Repeat trio exome sequencing at higher coverage to recheck UBE3A for missed point variants
Methylation-specific testing at the SNRPN locus (e.g., MS-MLPA), with SNP-array CMA to assess for UPD
Dedicated repeat-expansion testing for the FMR1 CGG repeat
Whole genome sequencing focused on deep-intronic regulatory variants in unrelated seizure genes
quiz.explanation: This is a classic Angelman syndrome picture — severe ID, absent speech, happy demeanor with laughter, ataxia, and epilepsy. Most Angelman cases are NOT due to a UBE3A point variant: they arise from a 15q11-q13 deletion, paternal UPD, or an imprinting defect, none of which are visible in sequence data alone. The right next step is methylation-specific testing at SNRPN (e.g., MS-MLPA), which detects the abnormal methylation pattern, paired with SNP-array CMA to identify UPD — the SNRPN methylation test detects roughly 80% of Angelman cases (and ~99% of Prader-Willi). A normal methylation result in this picture would then prompt UBE3A sequencing, but methylation comes first. Re-running exome cannot see a methylation/UPD defect. The FMR1 CGG repeat causes Fragile X, a different phenotype, and chasing unrelated intronic seizure genes ignores the recognizable imprinting syndrome in front of you.

quiz.question: A 4-month-old infant with an older sibling who died of spinal muscular atrophy is confirmed by molecular testing to have biallelic SMN1 loss but remains presymptomatic on exam. The parents ask how this diagnosis changes care. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only symptomatic/supportive care is available, so management does not change until weakness appears
SMN-restoring therapy is disease-modifying and most effective given presymptomatically, so treatment should be pursued now
Sodium-channel blockers are the cornerstone of SMA management and should be started immediately
Treatment should be deferred until the child develops weakness, because therapy cannot alter the natural history
quiz.explanation: SMA is a model of a disease-modifying diagnosis: SMN-restoring therapies — nusinersen (intrathecal ASO), risdiplam (oral SMN2 splicing modifier), and onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9-SMN1 gene replacement) — transform the natural history and are most effective when given presymptomatically, before motor neurons are lost. Waiting for weakness forfeits the window where these agents do the most good, so deferring is exactly wrong. 'Only supportive care' ignores that a precise molecular diagnosis is the gateway to these disease-modifying options. Sodium-channel blockers have no role in SMA — that drug-avoidance principle belongs to SCN1A/Dravet, a different disorder. This is why a confirmed molecular diagnosis reframes management rather than ending the workup.

quiz.question: An 8-year-old with confirmed tuberous sclerosis complex has a previously documented cardiac rhabdomyoma that has regressed and is now asymptomatic. Per the 2021 International TSC surveillance recommendations (Northrup et al.), which renal surveillance is indicated going forward?
options: Abdominal CT every year to monitor for angiomyolipoma
Renal MRI every 1–3 years, continued lifelong, to monitor for angiomyolipoma and cysts
Renal ultrasound only if hematuria or hypertension develops
No renal imaging is needed in childhood; begin renal surveillance only in adulthood
quiz.explanation: The Northrup 2021 TSC recommendations call for renal MRI every 1–3 years, continued lifelong, to monitor for angiomyolipoma and renal cysts — renal disease is a leading cause of TSC morbidity and mortality, so surveillance is not deferred to adulthood or made symptom-triggered. MRI, not CT, is the recommended modality, avoiding cumulative ionizing radiation, so annual abdominal CT is wrong on both modality and interval. Waiting for hematuria or hypertension abandons the point of a surveillance program, which is to detect lesions before complications. Note this scenario concerns the kidney specifically: the resolved cardiac rhabdomyoma is reassuring (echocardiography in asymptomatic children continues only until rhabdomyoma regression), but it does not change the lifelong renal MRI schedule.

quiz.question: A child has a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by a pathogenic variant confirmed to be de novo — absent from both parents' blood. The parents, planning another pregnancy, are told by an online source that their recurrence risk is 'zero' because neither of them carries it. How should the counselor frame the recurrence risk?
options: Confirm the risk is zero, since the variant was not found in either parent's blood
Counsel that recurrence risk is low but not zero — roughly ~1% for many neurodevelopmental conditions — because of possible parental germline (gonadal) mosaicism
Counsel a 50% recurrence risk, since the disorder is caused by an autosomal dominant variant
Counsel a 25% recurrence risk, treating the de novo variant as an autosomal recessive condition
quiz.explanation: After an apparently de novo variant (absent in both parents' blood), the empiric recurrence risk to a future pregnancy is low but NOT zero, because a parent can harbor germline (gonadal) mosaicism — the variant enriched in germ cells but undetectable in blood. A commonly cited figure is ~1% for many neurodevelopmental conditions, though it varies by disorder (e.g., ~0.5–1% for MECP2/Rett, but ~7–14% for DMD). Counseling 'zero' from negative parental blood alone is a classic and harmful error. The 50% and 25% figures describe inherited autosomal dominant and recessive transmission respectively, which do not apply when the variant is genuinely de novo rather than carried by a parent. For couples wanting to act on even this small risk, prenatal diagnosis and PGT-M with the known variant remain available options.
